criteria_results.title: §2(a): Restore 'entitlement order' language
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline expressly restores “Entitlement Order” in the definitions and adds it alongside “Instructions” in Section 2.2, with references to UCC Sections 8-106 and 9-104. This rejects the Bank’s instruction-only substitution and preserves the Article 8 control framework.

criteria_results.title: Cover note explains §2(a) entitlement order position
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover note expressly addresses the §2(a) “entitlement order” versus “instruction” change, rejects the Bank’s instruction-only substitution, and explains that restoring entitlement-order language preserves UCC Article 8 control protection and related perfection mechanics if an account is characterized as a securities account.

criteria_results.title: §2(b): Address springing exclusive control and reject broad Bank carve-out
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline preserves springing exclusive control upon delivery of a NOEC and expressly rejects unrestricted post-NOEC account operation. Sections 2.5 and 3.2 limit Graycliff’s operating rights to the pre-NOEC period and require the Bank, after receipt of a NOEC, to cease following Depositor instructions and comply exclusively with the Secured Party, subject only to limited treatment of transactions irrevocably initiated before receipt.

criteria_results.title: §3: Reject Bank set-off priority over Secured Party instructions
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline expressly deletes the Bank’s blanket set-off priority and restores a conflicting-instructions waterfall under which Secured Party instructions and entitlement orders prevail. It also states that permitted Bank set-off may not take priority over the Secured Party’s instructions or lien, including after a NOEC.

criteria_results.title: §4: Narrow expanded self-help set-off to direct, liquidated obligations
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.2 deletes the Bank’s broad set-off right covering direct or contingent and matured or unmatured obligations. It limits set-off to direct, matured, liquidated obligations arising under the deposit-account agreements, specifically customary account maintenance, service, transaction fees, and returned or charged-back items, while excluding contingent and unrelated financial-product exposures.

criteria_results.title: §5: Propose 3-business-day NOEC compliance period
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline proposes compliance with a NOEC no later than the third Business Day after receipt and authentication, expressly replacing the Bank’s five-Business-Day period and not reverting to the original two-Business-Day period.

criteria_results.title: §6: Reject indemnification coverage for Bank gross negligence
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.2 expressly deletes indemnification for losses arising from Bank negligence, including gross negligence, and replaces it with an exclusion for losses resulting from Bank's gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud, or material breach. It also states that no Secured Party indemnification is owed for Bank's own gross negligence or willful misconduct.

criteria_results.title: §7(a): Reject $50,000 aggregate liability cap
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline expressly deletes Section 7.1's $50,000 aggregate liability cap, and the cover note confirms Pinnacle's position is to delete the cap in its entirety.

criteria_results.title: §7(b): Address mutual consequential/punitive/indirect damages waiver
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline expressly addresses the mutual damages waiver in Section 7.2 by retaining a mutual waiver of indirect, consequential, incidental, special, punitive, and exemplary damages, while noting that Pinnacle reserves the right to revisit it. The cover note also explains this position.

criteria_results.title: Cover note confirms position on §7(b) mutual damages waiver
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover note expressly addresses the mutual consequential, punitive, and indirect damages waiver in item 8. It states that Pinnacle leaves the waiver in place for this turn, while reserving the right to revisit it based on the final liability and indemnification provisions.

criteria_results.title: §8: Reject 90-day lookback; propose full subordination or 180-day lookback
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline expressly rejects the Bank’s 90-day lookback in Section 5.1 and proposes full subordination of Bank liens, with a 180-day lookback as the minimum fallback. The cover note consistently reiterates rejection of the 90-day period and the proposed 180-day minimum.

criteria_results.title: §9: Reject 30-day unilateral termination; propose 90-day notice with transition rights
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.4 expressly deletes the Bank’s unilateral 30-day termination right and replaces it with termination only on at least 90 days’ prior written notice, coupled with Secured Party’s express right to transition the accounts and funds to a replacement bank and obtain a replacement control agreement. It also requires Bank cooperation and continued performance until the replacement arrangement is effective.

criteria_results.title: §10: Restore New York governing law
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.2 expressly deletes North Carolina governing law and restores New York governing law, with corresponding New York UCC references and forum provisions.

criteria_results.title: Cover note acknowledges New York governing law is strongly preferred with possible flexibility
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover note expressly addresses governing law and states that Pinnacle's position is to restore New York governing law and that its New York-law position is firm for this turn. This clearly indicates New York is strongly preferred, even though it does not expressly offer flexibility if it is a deal-breaker.

criteria_results.title: §12: Restore no-prior-control-agreement representation
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 12.1 restores the Bank’s representation that no other person has control over the Accounts, that Bank has not entered into and will not enter into another control or similar agreement without Secured Party consent, and that Bank has received no notice of any lien or adverse claim other than Secured Party’s lien.

criteria_results.title: §13: Restore successor-bank notification obligation
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline restores the successor-bank notification obligation in Section 8.1, requiring the Bank to give the Secured Party at least 30 days’ prior written notice before transferring the Accounts or its deposit-taking operations to a successor bank, and to obtain the successor’s written assumption of the Agreement.

criteria_results.title: §11: Accept annual maintenance fee but negotiate down $15,000 legal-fee reimbursement
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 11.1 accepts the $3,500 annual maintenance fee per account ($10,500 total), while Section 11.2 rejects the fixed $15,000 reimbursement and caps reimbursement at the lesser of $7,500 or actual documented outside legal fees.

criteria_results.title: ACA maintains form and substance satisfactory to Administrative Agent
criteria_results.reasoning: The redline preserves valid UCC control and perfection mechanics. It restores Entitlement Order language where Article 8 may apply, requires the Bank to follow Secured Party instructions without further Depositor consent, limits Depositor operation to the pre-NOEC period, cuts off Depositor rights following a NOEC subject only to limited processing mechanics, and rejects or materially limits the Bank’s asserted set-off and lien priority. It also deletes the liability cap and restores protections against competing control arrangements and termination gaps. No accepted Bank change materially compromises the Secured Party’s control.

criteria_results.title: Cover note maintains professional and cordial tone
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover note is formal, respectful, and appropriately firm for inter-counsel negotiations. It clearly identifies Pinnacle’s positions and rationale without using adversarial or informal language, and includes constructive phrasing such as “good-faith accommodation,” “practical middle ground,” and an invitation to arrange a call.
